title: Development charges complaint dismissed; accessibility plan endorsed
subtitle: Committee reviewed the 2023-2027 Accessibility Plan and heard a landowner's water main credit claim at 375 New Dundee Road.
overview: The Finance and Corporate Services Committee held a short meeting with two matters. It recommended approval of the City's 2023-2027 Accessibility Plan {{vote:m1}}, which sets out how the City will work to remove barriers to access for residents.

The committee also held a public hearing on a Development Charges Act complaint from the owner of a self-storage development at 375 New Dundee Road. The owner sought a credit of more than $222,000 for installing a 200mm water main, plus compensation for the land it occupies or City ownership of it. The committee recommended dismissing the complaint {{vote:m2}}, in line with the staff recommendation.

Both recommendations go to Council on February 27, 2023 for final ratification. The hearing result matters because it confirms how the City applies its development charge by-law and local service guidelines to privately installed water lines. A decision of the committee on a complaint can be appealed to the Ontario Land Tribunal.

decisions.detail: The committee recommended approving the 2023-2027 Accessibility Plan as the City of Kitchener's Accessibility Plan.

decisions.item: 375 New Dundee Road development charges complaint
decisions.detail: The committee recommended dismissing the Section 20 complaint about development charges imposed on the self-storage development at 375 New Dundee Road.

debate: On the accessibility plan, one councillor asked what the capital budget spending involved. Staff said there is an annual corporate accessibility fund of $75,000 for legislative requirements and one-time projects, such as 2022 improvements to a pool's parking and entrance.

The same councillor asked about recruiting people for other advisory committees. Staff said an earlier project was paused during the pandemic and is being reviewed alongside the equity committee's work plan.

The landowner's lawyers argued the City charged a water rate although no municipal water service reached the property line. They said the owner had to build a 200mm main at its own cost, which also benefits future development through a tee-connection. They relied on the credit provisions of the Development Charges Act.

Staff said a 200mm water line is a local service under the City's guidelines, not eligible for a development charge credit, and the developer's responsibility. They said the reduced rate already applied was the most suitable one available.

Staff also said the revised request for compensation for land and maintenance was received the Friday before the hearing and is not a remedy available under Section 20. They said the hearing was limited to whether the by-law was applied correctly, and their recommendation to dismiss did not change.
